note: What we're hearing — competitor mentions aggregated from Gong across open opportunities. Patterns and counts only. Never a customer name, a contact name, a deal name, or a verbatim quote. Generated by the weekly Gong sweep; human-editable via the admin sheet.
source: Gong, via CRM opportunities in Demo/Solution Evaluation
excluded: Ellis Partners appeared in 2 deals as an incumbent being replaced by PerformanceHQ, mostly over report turnaround. Ellis is a Grace Hill company, so this is an internal migration, not a competitive loss. Excluded from the counts below.
SkillCat appeared in 3 deals as a Grace Hill maintenance-certification add-on, not a competitor. Excluded from the counts below.

dealsWithCompetitorMention counts deals where a named vendor or outside alternative came up (Yardi Aspire, RealPage, an outside shop vendor, Interplay, and similar). It does not count status quo, Ellis, or SkillCat.

yardi-aspire.posture: Incumbent or prior source of training modules in all three. Not a fresh evaluation.
whatBuyersSay: Described as the incumbent for training and policies, with a team that is used to it and reluctant to change.
One buyer still assigns a few Aspire modules to new hires while running an in-house LMS.
One buyer said the Yardi classes cover assistant managers but lack leadership development content.
objectionsToUs: In one deal the team was burned by past Grace Hill-family mystery shops, and the buyer believes the recent improvements but the team has not seen them yet.
yardi-aspire.confirms: Inertia, not a feature gap, is what the buyer describes. The leadership-content gap matches the record.
yardi-aspire.useIt: Let them keep what Aspire does well. Ask what the team would build for leadership development today, and who owns that.

realpage-realconnect.posture: Current LMS in one deal, previously considered and dropped in the other.
whatBuyersSay: One buyer is dissatisfied with the RealPage LMS: unfulfilled promises and classes called boring and cartoonish. Their contract ends at the start of next year.
One buyer looked at RealPage Easy LMS and did not proceed over perceived quality.
realpage-realconnect.pricingSignal: No price figures. The contract end date in one deal is a switching window.
realpage-realconnect.confirms: Quality of content, not price, is what drove both buyers away from RealPage.
realpage-realconnect.useIt: Do not attack the platform. Ask what happens after a session ends — who records attendance, who proves competency, and how many places that data gets typed.

microsoft-sharepoint.posture: Incumbent storage, not a vendor evaluation.
whatBuyersSay: SharePoint or a handbook holds the buyer's SOPs and policies.
One buyer asked whether prior training records and existing policies can be imported.
microsoft-sharepoint.pricingSignal: None raised. It is already paid for, which is the whole difficulty.
microsoft-sharepoint.confirms: Exactly the displacement conversation the record describes — the fight is over version control and acknowledgment evidence, never document storage.
microsoft-sharepoint.useIt: Let them keep it for files. Ask who writes and updates the policy text today, and whether they could produce a timestamped acknowledgment per employee per version at audit.

status-quo-policies.posture: No vendor in the deal at all.
whatBuyersSay: Policies live in a paper handbook, and SOPs sit in a handbook or on a shared drive.
Outdated Word documents on an intranet serve as the only reference.
One buyer asked about a net-45 payment period and declining auto-renewal from the start.
objectionsToUs: Payment due at signing conflicts with one buyer's normal process.
status-quo-policies.pricingSignal: The status quo is free, so every conversation is a value case rather than a price comparison.
status-quo-policies.confirms: The status quo remains the most common thing we are actually replacing — more common in this sample than any named vendor.
status-quo-policies.useIt: Do not sell against the binder. Ask what happens when someone needs the answer at 4pm on a Friday, and how they would prove today what a departed employee was taught.

status-quo-training.posture: No vendor in the deal. Training is informal, in-house, or built from free resources.
whatBuyersSay: Shadowing, web searches, and insurer-provided toolbox sessions stand in for a program.
Two buyers run all training in-house. One described a prior employer's training as ineffective or nonexistent.
YouTube is used for problem-solving, with the buyer acknowledging the information is not always accurate.
One buyer asked whether their own how-to videos can be loaded into the custom course builder.
objectionsToUs: Extra logins matter: one buyer does not want to give about 200 employees another portal on top of an insurer's.
Two buyers asked about HRIS or single sign-on connections.
status-quo-training.pricingSignal: The status quo is free, so every conversation is a value case rather than a price comparison.
status-quo-training.confirms: Self-built training is among the most common things we replace, ahead of any named vendor.
status-quo-training.useIt: Do not sell against the free option. Ask how a new hire's training gets proven after the fact, and what it costs when someone does it wrong.

status-quo-mystery-shopping.posture: Mixed: spreadsheet tracking, outside vendors ordered through an internal contact, and one buyer going without shops.
whatBuyersSay: Spreadsheets track shops alongside onboarding and training completion.
One buyer is unhappy with an unnamed shop vendor and prefers going without, weighing AI and call-recording tools instead.
A buyer cited a lower per-shop price from a video-recorded vendor, with some concern about vetting and accuracy. Unverified.
objectionsToUs: Past experience with Grace Hill-family shops, mainly slow report turnaround.
Changing how internal stakeholders order and run shops.
A buyer asked what happens if the full shop volume in a commitment is not ordered.
status-quo-mystery-shopping.pricingSignal: Per-shop price and volume commitment came up in two deals. No vendor price is verified here.
status-quo-mystery-shopping.confirms: Shop alternatives show up as price and flexibility questions more than as a named rival. Not a single competing product in these deals.
status-quo-mystery-shopping.useIt: Ask what they do with a shop result once they have it, and whether they could compare this quarter to last year on the same questions.

eliseai.posture: Being implemented by the buyer. Grace Hill is a partner and some EliseAI content is available in the Grace Hill system.
whatBuyersSay: The buyer is implementing EliseAI alongside the evaluation.
eliseai.confirms: Supports the shopping angle — an AI answering layer changes what a shop is measuring, and creates a new thing to measure.
eliseai.useIt: Not a competitor here. Ask how they currently verify what the AI says to a prospect, and who owns the handoff when it escalates to a person.

surveymonkey.posture: Used for ad hoc surveys. Not a vendor evaluation.
whatBuyersSay: The buyer uses it for one-off surveys and confused a tenant-survey vendor with Kingsley.
surveymonkey.confirms: Ad hoc survey tools are in use at buyers who also want benchmarks.
surveymonkey.useIt: Ask how they compare results to peers. Kingsley benchmarks are the difference.

unmatched: Names heard this window that have no competitor record yet: Interplay (maintenance training, 2 deals, described as integrating with Grace Hill and not cheap), RBG (third-party shop vendor, 1 deal), NiceJob (reputation-management incumbent through a reseller arrangement, 1 deal). Cirrus was not named in any of the 40 deals reviewed.
